185328.name: Sorghum-Sudangrass Seed
185328.short_description: The fastest-establishing high-biomass cover crop available. Sorghum-sudangrass builds 4–8 tons of dry matter per acre in a single summer season, breaks hardpan compaction, and suppresses weeds naturally.
185328.description:
If you need to move serious organic matter in a hurry, sorghum-sudangrass is the tool. No other warm-season cover crop matches its combination of speed, biomass volume, and root penetration. Under good conditions it reaches 6–12 feet in 60–90 days, building 4–8 tons of dry matter per acre that decomposes into a thick mat of residue ideal for no-till cash crops.

The root system is where this grass really earns its keep. A dense, fibrous network drives 3 feet or more into compacted subsoil layers, physically fracturing hardpan without a single tillage pass. Farmers dealing with wheel-track compaction, plow pans, or degraded subsoil structure use sorghum-sudangrass as the primary rehabilitation tool before transitioning to no-till or reduced-till systems.

Sorghum-sudangrass is also allelopathic. It releases biochemical compounds that inhibit weed seed germination in the surrounding soil—a practical, chemical-free suppression mechanism that benefits the following cash crop, especially transplanted vegetables and small grains.

There are real limitations and you need to know them before you plant. This crop produces dhurrin, which converts to prussic acid (hydrogen cyanide) when plant tissue is stressed—by drought, frost, or mechanical damage. Do not graze plants under 18 inches tall, and do not graze drought-stressed plants — wait 7–10 days after a frost-kill event or after drought stress is relieved. Sorghum-sudangrass can also accumulate toxic nitrate levels under drought or heavy nitrogen fertilization, a hazard separate from prussic acid; test forage if conditions warrant. These are not theoretical risks; they are documented livestock toxicity events. The crop also requires warm soil (65°F minimum) to germinate and cannot survive frost. Terminating and incorporating the heavy biomass requires equipment capable of handling tall, dense material.

Sorghum-sudangrass is a purpose-built summer workhorse for farmers who need maximum soil improvement in minimum time. Planted right, it earns its spot in any rotation.

184687.name: Indiangrass Seed
categories: Northern US Pasture Seeds & Seed Mixes
Transitional Zone Pasture Seeds & Seed Mixes
184687.short_description: The showiest grass of the tallgrass prairie. Indiangrass produces golden seed heads with turquoise anthers in bloom and delivers excellent forage quality that holds late into the season, strong carbon sequestration credentials, and proven CRP performance across zones 4-9.
184687.description: Indiangrass is the second-most dominant species of the original North American tallgrass prairie, almost always found growing alongside Big Bluestem in the deep-soil lowlands and mesic uplands that once defined the Great Plains. Sorghastrum nutans is botanically distinct among the tallgrass species — in midsummer bloom, it produces golden-brown seed heads with brilliant turquoise-blue anthers that are unmistakable at a distance. It is the most visually dramatic native grass in bloom of any tallgrass species. For livestock producers, Indiangrass is a highly palatable, high-quality forage — NRCS rates it among the more nutritious native prairie grasses, on par with Big Bluestem. Cattle graze it readily through the growing season, and it holds acceptable quality well into maturity. In native hay systems, Indiangrass is commonly cut at the boot stage for premium quality. Root depth of 5 to 8 feet gives it strong drought tolerance and significant carbon sequestration potential, placing it on approved species lists for NRCS carbon programs. In prairie restoration plantings, Indiangrass is almost always seeded in combination with Big Bluestem, Switchgrass, and Little Bluestem rather than as a monoculture. The two dominant tallgrass species complement each other's phenology and growth habits — a mixed native stand produces more consistent forage across the season than either species alone, and provides higher wildlife habitat complexity. Indiangrass is hardy in zones 4 through 9 and performs well across a broad geographic range from the upper Midwest through the Gulf Coast. Its adaptation is somewhat narrower than Big Bluestem on highly droughty or sandy soils, but on medium to heavy soils in adequate rainfall zones, it is a premier native grass for every use from CRP to conservation landscaping.

184658.name: Sideoats Grama Grass Seed
categories: Southern US Pasture Seeds & Seed Mixes
Transitional Zone Pasture Seeds & Seed Mixes
184658.short_description: The Texas state grass and one of the most widespread native grasses in North America. Sideoats Grama thrives on rocky, alkaline, and shallow soils from Canada to Mexico — and establishes faster than most other native prairie species.
184658.description:
Sideoats Grama is the official state grass of Texas and one of the most geographically expansive native grasses on the continent, documented from Saskatchewan, Canada to the high plateaus of Mexico. Bouteloua curtipendula earns its common name from the distinctive pendulous seed heads in which small oat-like florets hang down one side of each stem — a seed structure that is unmistakable in the field and gives the plant ornamental character unlike any other native grass.

For producers and conservationists working on thin, rocky, alkaline, or shallow soils, Sideoats Grama is frequently the best available native warm-season option. Where Big Bluestem and Indiangrass struggle on droughty uplands or calcareous soils, Sideoats Grama performs reliably. It tolerates a wider pH range, a more extreme drought cycle, and shallower soils than the taller tallgrass species, which is why it dominates the rocky hillsides and short-grass transition zones of the southern and central Plains.

Germination and establishment are meaningfully better than other native prairie grasses. Unlike Big Bluestem and Indiangrass, which commonly show almost no visible growth in year 1, Sideoats Grama often establishes visibly in the seeding year — giving producers confidence the stand is working. Full production still requires 2 seasons, but the establishment timeline is compressed compared to the tallgrass species.

Forage quality is good across the season. Cattle graze Sideoats Grama willingly through early and mid-season, and it maintains reasonable palatability through maturity compared to the tallgrass species. On marginal upland sites in the southern and central Plains, it may be the highest-yielding native forage option available.

Sideoats Grama is heavily specified in Texas Wildscape programs, state grass rebate kits, xeriscape plantings, and roadside naturalization projects across the south-central Plains — a reflection of its versatility across use cases from restoration to erosion control to ornamental.

Plant in early spring to trap residual nutrients, prevent erosion, and improve soil structure while creating a thriving green cover that feeds beneficial soil biology. It works well in rotations with vegetables and field crops, aligning with sustainable farming practices and organic standards. Use Crimson Clover as a short-term cover crop to reduce synthetic inputs, improve seedbed quality, and support healthier yields in the next crop.

This seed supports longer grazing periods, improves legume balance in pastures, and enhances soil health through nitrogen fixation. It adapts to a range of soils and climates, making it a reliable choice for rotational grazing, early-season feed, or drought-resilient forage. Choose Red Clover Seed for productive, sustainable forage and dependable hay harvests.
